title: Epilepsy & Seizures
summary: Classifying seizures, finding their cause, and treating them.

lessons.title: Seizure Classification

levels.kid:
Your brain cells talk using tiny electric sparks. Usually they take turns, like people in a good conversation. In a seizure, lots of cells suddenly shout at the same time, all together, and the brain gets jammed for a little while.

Some seizures start in one small spot, like one corner of a room shouting. Others start everywhere at once.

A seizure can make someone shake, stare, or act a bit strange for a minute. Most stop on their own. If someone has one, keep them safe, put nothing in their mouth, and time it.
levels.hs:
A seizure is a brief episode of abnormal, excessive, synchronized electrical activity in the brain that causes symptoms. Epilepsy is a condition of recurring, unprovoked seizures. Having one seizure does not mean someone has epilepsy.

The International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) classifies seizures by where they start:
- Focal onset: starts in one network on one side of the brain. Described by awareness: focal aware (the person knows what is happening) or focal impaired awareness (they are confused or don't remember). Symptoms depend on the location: jerking of one hand, a strange smell, a rising feeling in the stomach, or lip-smacking.
- Generalized onset: starts in networks on both sides at once. Types include tonic-clonic (stiffening, then rhythmic jerking), absence (brief staring spells, common in children), myoclonic (quick jerks), atonic (sudden loss of muscle tone, causing falls) and tonic (stiffening).
- Unknown onset: when nobody saw how it began.

A focal seizure can spread to both sides and become a 'focal to bilateral tonic-clonic' seizure.

Seizures can be provoked by things like low blood sugar, low sodium, fever in young children, or a head injury. These are called acute symptomatic seizures.

After a seizure, people are often confused or sleepy. This is the postictal state. Some have temporary weakness on one side, called Todd's paralysis.

First aid: time it, protect the head, turn them on their side, and call emergency services if it lasts more than five minutes.
levels.college:
Definitions (ILAE): a seizure is a transient occurrence of signs and/or symptoms due to abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity. Epilepsy is diagnosed with at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60 percent over ten years (for example with an epileptiform EEG or a structural lesion), or diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome.

The 2017 classification sorts seizures by onset:
- Focal: classified by awareness, then by first prominent sign: motor (automatisms, clonic, tonic, hyperkinetic, epileptic spasms) or non-motor (sensory, cognitive, emotional, autonomic, behavior arrest). Location predicts semiology: mesial temporal seizures often begin with a rising epigastric sensation or déjà vu, then oral and manual automatisms; frontal seizures are brief, nocturnal and hyperkinetic; occipital seizures produce visual phenomena; parietal seizures produce sensory symptoms.
- Generalized: motor (tonic-clonic, clonic, tonic, myoclonic, myoclonic-tonic-clonic, myoclonic-atonic, atonic, epileptic spasms) or non-motor (typical absence, atypical absence, myoclonic absence, eyelid myoclonia).
- Unknown onset.

The classification then proceeds to epilepsy type (focal, generalized, combined, unknown) and syndrome, with etiology categories: structural, genetic, infectious, metabolic, immune and unknown.

Key distinctions:
- Absence vs focal impaired awareness: absence seizures last seconds, start and stop abruptly, have no postictal confusion and are triggered by hyperventilation; focal seizures last longer and are followed by confusion.
- Seizure vs syncope: syncope usually has a trigger (standing, pain), pallor, brief jerks, and rapid recovery without prolonged confusion. A bitten side of the tongue favors seizure.
- Functional (psychogenic nonepileptic) seizures: eyes often closed, side-to-side head movement, waxing and waning; video-EEG distinguishes them.
levels.phd:
Seizures emerge when the balance of excitation and inhibition in a network tips into hypersynchrony. Mechanisms operate at several scales.

Cellular: the paroxysmal depolarization shift, first recorded in experimental foci, is a large calcium-dependent depolarization driving a burst of action potentials, followed by hyperpolarization. Synchronous paroxysmal depolarization shifts across a population produce the interictal spike. Transition to a seizure involves failure of surround inhibition, depolarization block of interneurons, extracellular potassium accumulation, and chloride loading that shifts GABA-A responses toward depolarization.

Focal onset patterns on intracranial EEG include low-voltage fast activity, thought to reflect interneuron-driven onset, and hypersynchronous onset, more typical of mesial temporal sclerosis. Seizure termination is an active process involving adenosine release, potassium-channel activation, ATP depletion and neuromodulator shifts, which may explain postictal suppression.

Generalized absence seizures arise from thalamocortical circuits. T-type calcium channels in thalamic relay neurons generate rebound bursts after hyperpolarization by the reticular nucleus, producing the 3 hertz spike-and-wave rhythm. This explains why ethosuximide, which blocks T-type channels, treats absence but not focal seizures. The cortical focus theory, from rodent models such as the WAG/Rij rat, adds that absence discharges may begin in a somatosensory cortical region and recruit the thalamus.

The classification itself encodes a conceptual shift: from regarding seizures as 'focal versus generalized' structures to describing networks. Many 'generalized' epilepsies have focal features, and 'focal' seizures recruit widespread networks. Network theory models epilepsy as a disease of connectivity, with interictal hubs and seizure-onset zones as nodes. This framing influences surgery: removing the onset zone may fail if seizures arise from a distributed network, which motivates neuromodulation. Computational models, such as the Epileptor, describe seizures as transitions between dynamical states governed by slow variables.
levels.expert:
Classification is a bedside skill: the history from a witness is the most important diagnostic test, more important than any scan.

What to ask:
- What happened right before? A warning (aura) points to focal onset, and the aura's content points to a location.
- What did it look like? Head turning, posture, which limb jerked first, eyes open or closed, duration.
- How did they recover? Prolonged confusion favors a seizure; quick recovery favors syncope.
- Was there tongue biting (lateral), incontinence, injury?
- Any triggers: sleep deprivation, flashing lights, missed medications, fever, illness?
- Previous subtle episodes: morning jerks dropping a toothbrush (myoclonus), staring spells, déjà vu attacks.

Pitfalls attendings watch for:
- Convulsive syncope: brief jerks are common in fainting and are often mislabeled as seizures. Ask about posture, pallor and prodrome, and get an ECG, because cardiac syncope can kill.
- Treating every first seizure: after a single unprovoked seizure, recurrence risk is moderate, and treatment reduces early recurrence but does not change long-term remission. The decision is individualized with the patient.
- Missing a provoked cause: check glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium, toxins and infection.
- Driving: most jurisdictions restrict driving after a seizure for a defined seizure-free period. Counseling on this and on water safety is part of the visit.

Workup after a first unprovoked seizure in an adult: EEG (ideally within 48 hours or with sleep deprivation, which increases yield) and MRI with an epilepsy protocol. In a neurosurgical context, semiology is used to generate a hypothesis about where seizures begin, then tested against EEG, MRI and other studies. A seizure with early head version to one side, for example, usually points to the opposite hemisphere.

keyPoints: Seizure = transient symptoms from abnormal synchronous neuronal activity; epilepsy = enduring predisposition.
ILAE: focal, generalized or unknown onset; focal seizures described by awareness.
Focal seizures can evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic.
Absence seizures: brief, abrupt, no postictal confusion; 3 Hz spike-and-wave.
Distinguish from syncope and functional seizures; the witness history is key.
Epilepsy: two unprovoked seizures >24 h apart, or one with ≥60% recurrence risk, or a syndrome.

lessons.title: Epilepsy Syndromes

levels.kid:
Epilepsy comes in different kinds, a bit like how there are different kinds of dogs. Each kind has its own age when it usually starts, its own type of seizures, and its own pattern on a brain-wave test.

Some kinds happen in young kids and go away as they grow up. Some kinds start in teenagers, with little jerks in the morning. A few kinds are very serious and start in babies.

Knowing the exact kind helps doctors pick the best medicine and tell families what to expect, like whether it will likely go away by itself.
levels.hs:
An epilepsy syndrome is a recognizable pattern: a typical age of onset, seizure types, EEG findings, and often a known cause and outlook. Naming the syndrome guides treatment.

Some important syndromes:
- Childhood absence epilepsy: starts around ages 4 to 10, with many brief staring spells a day. Most children outgrow it.
- Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME): starts in the teen years. Morning jerks, often making someone drop things, plus generalized tonic-clonic seizures, especially after poor sleep. Usually lifelong but well controlled with the right medicine.
- Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (once called benign rolandic epilepsy): school-age kids have seizures at night involving one side of the face and mouth, sometimes drooling or trouble speaking. It goes away by the teens.
- Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (including West syndrome): babies have clusters of sudden flexing or extending movements, often on waking. It is an emergency because development can stall without fast treatment.
- Dravet syndrome: starts in the first year with long seizures, often with fever. Usually caused by a gene change in a sodium channel. Some common seizure medicines make it worse.
- Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: childhood onset, many seizure types including drop attacks, intellectual disability, and a slow spike-wave EEG.
- Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis: the most common epilepsy treated with surgery in adults.

Febrile seizures, seizures with fever in children from about 6 months to 5 years, are common and usually harmless, and most are not epilepsy.
levels.college:
Syndrome diagnosis integrates age, semiology, EEG, imaging, genetics and comorbidity, and matters for drug choice because some drugs aggravate certain syndromes.

Generalized syndromes (idiopathic generalized epilepsies):
- Childhood absence epilepsy: 3 Hz generalized spike-wave provoked by hyperventilation. Ethosuximide is first choice when absence is the only seizure type; valproate and lamotrigine are alternatives.
- Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: 4 to 6 Hz generalized polyspike-wave, photosensitivity in many. Valproate is highly effective but avoided when possible in girls and women who could become pregnant because of birth defect and neurodevelopmental risks; levetiracetam and lamotrigine are alternatives (lamotrigine can worsen myoclonus in some). Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and phenytoin can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures.

Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs), where epileptic activity and the underlying cause both impair development:
- Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome: hypsarrhythmia on EEG (chaotic, high-amplitude, multifocal). First-line hormonal therapy (ACTH or high-dose oral steroids) or vigabatrin, especially for tuberous sclerosis complex.
- Dravet syndrome: SCN1A loss of function, mostly de novo. Sodium channel blockers worsen seizures. Treatments include valproate, clobazam, stiripentol and fenfluramine.
- Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: tonic seizures in sleep, atypical absences, atonic drops; slow (under 2.5 Hz) spike-wave and generalized paroxysmal fast activity in sleep. Rufinamide and clobazam are among options; corpus callosotomy for drop attacks.

Focal syndromes:
- Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes: sleep-activated centrotemporal spikes; often no treatment needed.
- Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis: hippocampal atrophy and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity on MRI; often a history of prolonged febrile seizures in early childhood; frequently drug-resistant but highly surgically treatable.

Genetic testing is now routine for DEEs and infant-onset epilepsy, as results can change therapy and counseling.
levels.phd:
Syndromes are increasingly mapped onto molecular mechanisms, and the most instructive example is Dravet syndrome. SCN1A encodes Nav1.1, a sodium channel enriched in fast-spiking GABAergic interneurons, particularly parvalbumin-positive cells. Haploinsufficiency impairs interneuron firing more than pyramidal cell firing, producing net disinhibition. This explains the paradox that sodium channel blockers, which further reduce Nav1.1 function in interneurons, aggravate seizures. It also motivates precision therapy: antisense oligonucleotides that exploit a 'poison exon' in SCN1A to increase productive transcript from the healthy allele (targeted augmentation of nuclear gene output) are in clinical trials and have shown seizure reduction.

By contrast, gain-of-function SCN2A and SCN8A variants, which increase excitatory neuron firing, can respond to sodium channel blockers. Other genes reveal different mechanisms: KCNQ2 encephalopathy (potassium M-current loss), STXBP1 (synaptic vesicle release), CDKL5, PCDH19 (X-linked with female-limited expression from cellular mosaicism) and GRIN2A, which links to the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum. Tuberous sclerosis complex, caused by TSC1 or TSC2 loss with mTOR overactivation, makes the mTOR inhibitor everolimus a mechanism-based therapy for refractory seizures.

The idiopathic generalized epilepsies are mostly polygenic. Genome-wide studies show they carry a high burden of common variants, with shared heritability across generalized syndromes, and polygenic risk scores distinguish generalized from focal epilepsy at the population level.

Mesial temporal sclerosis raises a chicken-and-egg question: whether prolonged febrile seizures cause hippocampal sclerosis or whether a pre-existing abnormality causes both. Prospective studies such as FEBSTAT showed that some children develop acute hippocampal T2 signal changes after febrile status epilepticus, with some progressing to sclerosis, supporting at least a partial causal role.

The ILAE's 2022 syndrome definitions introduced 'self-limited' instead of 'benign' and grouped syndromes by age of onset, recognizing that labels shape expectations for families.
levels.expert:
Getting the syndrome right is one of the highest-yield things a clinician does in epilepsy, because the wrong drug can worsen seizures for years.

Patterns to recognize quickly:
- A teenager with morning jerks that make them spill drinks, and a tonic-clonic seizure after a sleepover: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Ask directly about morning jerks, as patients rarely volunteer them. Avoid carbamazepine and other narrow-spectrum sodium channel drugs. Counsel about sleep regularity. Discuss valproate's pregnancy risks openly, which affects drug choice in girls and young women.
- An infant with clusters of brief flexion spasms on waking and loss of social smiles: obtain an EEG within days and start treatment quickly; time to treatment affects developmental outcome. Look for tuberous sclerosis with a skin exam using a Wood's lamp for ash-leaf spots.
- A baby with prolonged febrile and afebrile hemiclonic seizures in the first year, triggered by warm baths: think Dravet. Send genetic testing and avoid sodium channel blockers. Families need a rescue plan, because prolonged seizures are common, and counseling about sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP).
- A school-age child with nocturnal facial twitching and drooling, normal development, and centrotemporal spikes: reassure. Many need no medicine.

Treatment-resistant syndromes deserve surgical thinking early. Lennox-Gastaut patients with injurious drop attacks may benefit from corpus callosotomy or vagus nerve stimulation. A child with an epileptic encephalopathy from one structural lesion may achieve dramatic developmental gains after resection or hemispherotomy, even when the EEG looks generalized. In mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, surgery is the evidence-based standard once two appropriate drugs have failed.

Always reassess the diagnosis when 'epilepsy' does not respond as expected: is it the right syndrome, or epilepsy at all?

keyPoints: An epilepsy syndrome bundles age of onset, seizure types, EEG, cause and prognosis.
JME: teen-onset morning myoclonus + GTCs, polyspike-wave; carbamazepine can aggravate it.
Infantile spasms + hypsarrhythmia: urgent treatment with hormones or vigabatrin.
Dravet: SCN1A loss of function; sodium channel blockers worsen seizures.
Lennox-Gastaut: multiple seizure types, tonic seizures in sleep, slow spike-wave.
Mesial temporal sclerosis: common, often drug-resistant, highly treatable with surgery.

lessons.title: EEG

levels.kid:
An EEG is a way to listen to the brain's electricity. Doctors stick little sensors on your head with sticky paste. Each sensor is like a tiny microphone that hears the brain humming.

The computer draws the hum as wiggly lines. When you are awake and calm with your eyes closed, the lines make a smooth, even rhythm. When you sleep, they get slower and bigger.

If a brain has seizures, the lines may show sharp pointy spikes. It doesn't hurt at all, and it helps doctors understand what the brain is doing.
levels.hs:
An electroencephalogram (EEG) records the brain's electrical activity through electrodes on the scalp. The signals come mostly from many cortical neurons near the surface acting together. A single neuron is far too weak to detect.

Brain waves are described by frequency, meaning cycles per second (hertz):
- Delta (under 4 Hz): deep sleep; abnormal in awake adults.
- Theta (4 to 7 Hz): drowsiness; common in children.
- Alpha (8 to 12 Hz): relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed, strongest at the back of the head. It fades when the eyes open.
- Beta (over 13 Hz): active thinking, alertness, and some medicines such as benzodiazepines.

In epilepsy, the EEG can show epileptiform discharges between seizures: spikes, sharp waves and spike-and-wave complexes. These support the diagnosis and help show whether seizures are focal or generalized. During a seizure, the EEG shows an evolving rhythmic pattern.

But a normal routine EEG does not rule out epilepsy. A routine study lasts about 20 to 40 minutes, and the abnormal activity may not appear then. Repeating it, recording sleep, or doing a longer study increases the chance of catching something.

Technicians use 'activation procedures': deep breathing (hyperventilation), which can trigger absence seizures, and flashing lights (photic stimulation), which can trigger some generalized epilepsies.

EEG is also used in intensive care to detect hidden seizures in unconscious patients.
levels.college:
Technical basics: electrodes are placed by the international 10-20 system. Displayed 'montages' compare electrode pairs (bipolar) or each electrode to a reference (referential). In a bipolar chain, a focal negative discharge produces 'phase reversal' at the electrode closest to the source.

The EEG signal reflects summed postsynaptic potentials of vertically oriented pyramidal neurons; action potentials contribute little. Roughly 6 square centimeters or more of synchronously active cortex is needed for a spike to appear on scalp EEG, which is why many deep or small discharges are invisible.

Normal features: posterior dominant rhythm (alpha, reactive to eye opening), mu rhythm over motor cortex, sleep architecture (vertex waves, sleep spindles, K-complexes in stage N2, slow waves in N3).

Abnormal findings:
- Focal slowing: suggests a structural lesion or dysfunction underneath.
- Interictal epileptiform discharges: spikes (20 to 70 milliseconds), sharp waves (70 to 200 milliseconds), spike-and-wave complexes. Location suggests the epileptogenic region.
- Generalized patterns: 3 Hz spike-wave (absence), polyspike-wave (JME), slow spike-wave (Lennox-Gastaut), hypsarrhythmia (infantile spasms).
- Encephalopathy patterns: diffuse slowing, triphasic waves (classically hepatic), burst suppression (severe dysfunction, anesthesia or hypothermia).
- Periodic and rhythmic patterns in critically ill patients, described with American Clinical Neurophysiology Society terminology: lateralized periodic discharges (LPDs), generalized periodic discharges (GPDs), lateralized and generalized rhythmic delta activity. They lie on the ictal-interictal continuum.

Benign variants that mimic epileptiform activity are a major source of misdiagnosis: wicket spikes, small sharp spikes, 14 and 6 Hz positive spikes, and rhythmic midtemporal theta of drowsiness.

Sensitivity: a first routine EEG detects interictal discharges in about a third to a half of people with epilepsy; serial and sleep-deprived recordings raise yield. Video-EEG monitoring captures events to classify them and to localize seizures for surgery.
levels.phd:
Scalp EEG measures an aggregate potential produced mainly by synaptic currents flowing along apical dendrites of cortical pyramidal cells, whose parallel arrangement creates open-field dipoles. Tangential and radial dipole orientations determine which scalp regions show a discharge, and a spike from a sulcal wall may project its maximum away from its true source. The skull acts as a low-pass spatial filter, smearing signals, which is why source localization requires inverse modeling with realistic head models. The inverse problem has no unique solution, so assumptions such as distributed sources with minimum norm or equivalent current dipoles constrain it.

Rhythms arise from network mechanisms. Alpha reflects thalamocortical and cortico-cortical loops and has been linked to functional inhibition of task-irrelevant regions. Sleep spindles originate in the thalamic reticular nucleus. Gamma oscillations depend on fast-spiking interneurons and are implicated in binding and attention.

In epilepsy research, high-frequency oscillations (ripples of 80 to 250 Hz and fast ripples of 250 to 500 Hz) recorded intracranially have been proposed as biomarkers of the epileptogenic zone. Early surgical series suggested removing fast-ripple regions improved outcome, but a randomized trial (HFO trial) found tailoring surgery by HFOs was not superior to standard spike-based tailoring, tempering enthusiasm. Interictal spikes themselves are not innocent: they transiently disrupt cognition, and hippocampal spikes during sleep can interfere with memory consolidation by competing with physiological sharp-wave ripples.

Quantitative EEG in the ICU uses compressed spectral arrays and other trends to screen many hours for seizures and detect delayed cerebral ischemia after SAH through loss of fast frequencies. Machine-learning spike detectors now approach expert-level performance on some datasets. A key frontier is distinguishing true ictal patterns from the ictal-interictal continuum: periodic discharges with high frequency or 'plus' features carry seizure risk, but whether treating them improves outcome remains under study.
levels.expert:
Two errors define bad EEG practice: overreading and underusing.

Overreading is the classic cause of epilepsy misdiagnosis. Normal variants, drowsiness patterns and artifacts (eye movements, muscle, electrode pops, ECG) are reported as 'sharp waves', and a patient with syncope or functional seizures is labeled with epilepsy and put on medicines for years. Rules of thumb:
- Treat the patient, not the EEG. An 'abnormal' EEG without a convincing clinical event is not epilepsy.
- Ask whether a reported discharge disrupts the background, has an aftergoing slow wave and a plausible field. Isolated sharp transients in drowsiness are often benign.
- Remember that some healthy people, especially relatives of people with epilepsy, show epileptiform discharges without ever having seizures.

Underusing EEG harms patients too:
- In the ICU, nonconvulsive seizures and nonconvulsive status epilepticus are common in comatose patients after cardiac arrest, trauma, hemorrhage and sepsis. Unexplained decreased consciousness warrants continuous EEG, because a routine study may miss them.
- After convulsive status epilepticus, a patient who doesn't wake up should be monitored, since ongoing electrographic seizures are frequent.
- In first-seizure clinics, a sleep-deprived EEG increases yield.

For the epilepsy surgery pathway, video-EEG monitoring is essential. Medicines are tapered to capture habitual seizures, the semiology on video is compared with the EEG onset, and patients' typical events must be confirmed as epileptic. When scalp EEG and imaging don't agree, intracranial recording with stereo-EEG depth electrodes or subdural grids defines the onset zone and maps eloquent cortex through stimulation. A neurosurgeon must be able to read these recordings, because the plan for resection depends on them.

keyPoints: EEG records summed postsynaptic potentials of cortical pyramidal neurons.
Bands: delta <4, theta 4-7, alpha 8-12 (posterior, eyes closed), beta >13 Hz.
Interictal spikes and sharp waves support epilepsy; a normal EEG does not exclude it.
Activation: hyperventilation, photic stimulation, sleep deprivation.

lessons.title: Status Epilepticus

levels.kid:
Most seizures stop by themselves in a minute or two, like a sneeze that ends. But sometimes the brain gets stuck in seizure mode and can't stop. That is called status epilepticus.

It is an emergency, like a fire alarm that won't turn off. The longer it goes, the harder it is to stop and the more it can hurt the brain.

Doctors act fast. First they make sure the person can breathe. Then they give medicines one after another to calm the brain down, and they look for what started it.
levels.hs:
Status epilepticus (SE) is a seizure that lasts too long, or repeated seizures without recovery in between. For convulsive (tonic-clonic) seizures, treatment should begin at 5 minutes, because seizures that last that long are unlikely to stop on their own. After about 30 minutes, lasting brain injury becomes more likely.

Why do seizures become self-sustaining? The brain's 'brakes' fail. During a long seizure, GABA receptors, which normally calm neurons, are pulled inside the cells and stop working, while more excitatory glutamate receptors move to the surface. That is why the first medicines work best if given early.

Common causes:
- In people with epilepsy, missed or stopped medications.
- Stroke, head injury, brain infections, tumors.
- Low blood sugar, low sodium, toxins, or suddenly stopping certain medicines.
- Autoimmune encephalitis.

Treatment happens in stages:
1. Stabilize: airway, breathing, circulation; check blood sugar.
2. First-line: a benzodiazepine, such as lorazepam into a vein, or midazolam into a muscle or the nose when there is no IV.
3. Second-line: an IV seizure medicine such as levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate.
4. If seizures continue: anesthetic drugs in intensive care with continuous EEG.

There is also nonconvulsive status epilepticus: ongoing seizure activity without obvious shaking, seen as confusion or coma. It can only be confirmed with an EEG.
levels.college:
The ILAE 2015 definition uses two time points: t1, when the seizure is considered prolonged and treatment should start, and t2, when long-term consequences become likely. For convulsive SE, t1 is 5 minutes and t2 is 30 minutes. For focal SE with impaired awareness, t1 is 10 minutes and t2 longer than 60 minutes. For absence SE, t1 is 10 to 15 minutes and t2 is unknown.

Stages and evidence:
- Early SE: benzodiazepines. The RAMPART trial showed intramuscular midazolam was at least as effective as IV lorazepam in the prehospital setting, because it can be given faster. A key error is underdosing or delaying benzodiazepines.
- Established (benzodiazepine-refractory) SE: the ESETT trial compared levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate and found them similarly effective, each stopping seizures in about half of patients.
- Refractory SE: persists after first and second-line drugs. Treated with continuous infusions of midazolam, propofol or pentobarbital in the ICU, titrated to seizure suppression or burst suppression on continuous EEG.
- Super-refractory SE: continues 24 hours or more after anesthesia, or recurs on weaning.

New-onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE) is refractory SE without a known epilepsy or immediately clear cause; FIRES is a subset preceded by fever. About half of NORSE cases with an identified cause are autoimmune, so immunotherapy is often started early.

Workup in parallel with treatment: glucose, electrolytes including sodium, calcium and magnesium, kidney and liver function, toxicology, drug levels in known epilepsy, blood count, cultures, CT and later MRI, lumbar puncture if infection or autoimmune disease is possible, and EEG. Give thiamine before glucose when malnutrition is possible.

Complications: hypoxia, aspiration, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, lactic acidosis, cardiac arrhythmias and neuronal injury. Mortality in adults is substantial and depends mostly on cause and age.
levels.phd:
The transition from a self-limited seizure to self-sustaining SE involves receptor trafficking. Within minutes of continuous seizure activity, synaptic GABA-A receptors containing beta-2/3 and gamma-2 subunits undergo clathrin-dependent endocytosis, reducing inhibitory synaptic currents. Simultaneously, NMDA and calcium-permeable AMPA receptors are trafficked to the synaptic membrane. The time-dependent pharmacoresistance this produces is well documented: benzodiazepine potency drops many-fold as seizures continue in animal models, providing the scientific basis for treating early and aggressively.

This biology suggests rational polytherapy for late SE: combining a GABA-A modulator with an NMDA antagonist to restore the inhibitory-excitatory balance. Animal studies show strong synergy for such combinations, and several NMDA receptor blockers have been tested in models. Some neurosteroids act on extrasynaptic GABA-A receptors (containing delta subunits) that are not internalized, which motivated a trial of the neurosteroid ganaxolone in refractory SE.

Neuronal injury in prolonged SE is largely excitotoxic: calcium entry triggers mitochondrial failure, oxidative stress and both necrotic and apoptotic death, even when systemic factors like hypoxia are controlled, as shown by Meldrum's classic experiments in paralyzed, ventilated baboons. Prolonged SE also triggers neuroinflammation, with interleukin-1-beta and high-mobility group box 1 signaling, and blood-brain barrier disruption with albumin extravasation activating astrocytic TGF-beta signaling, which may contribute to later epileptogenesis.

For NORSE and FIRES, the cytokine hypothesis has clinical consequences. Elevated interleukin-6 and interleukin-1 pathway activity motivate trials of anakinra (an IL-1 receptor antagonist) and tocilizumab (an IL-6 receptor blocker). Case series suggest benefit, especially with early use, but randomized evidence is lacking.

The ESETT result, three mechanistically different drugs with similar efficacy, also raises the question of whether refractoriness reflects drug mechanism or the underlying cause.
levels.expert:
Treat status epilepticus like a cardiac arrest: a protocol, a clock, and a team leader.

The working algorithm:
- 0 to 5 minutes: ABCs, oxygen, monitoring, finger-stick glucose, IV access. Give thiamine and glucose if hypoglycemic or at risk.
- 5 to 20 minutes: a full, weight-based dose of a benzodiazepine, repeated once if needed. Underdosing benzodiazepines out of fear of respiratory depression is one of the most common errors, and untreated SE itself causes respiratory failure.
- 20 to 40 minutes: a second-line IV drug. Choose based on the patient: valproate is avoided in liver disease, mitochondrial disorders and pregnancy; fosphenytoin needs cardiac monitoring; levetiracetam is simple with few interactions.
- After 40 minutes or failure of second-line: intubation, an anesthetic infusion and continuous EEG.

Pearls:
- A patient who stops shaking but doesn't wake within about 20 to 30 minutes may still be seizing. Get an EEG; subtle twitching of the eyes or a finger can be the only sign.
- Look for and treat the cause at the same time: hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, infection, a new bleed or tumor. In a young woman with psychiatric symptoms, abnormal movements and refractory SE, think of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis and look for an ovarian teratoma.
- Functional (psychogenic) seizures can mimic SE; eyes forced shut, side-to-side movements and resistance to eye opening are clues. Intubating a patient with functional seizures causes real harm, but when in doubt, treat as epileptic until EEG clarifies.
- In children, intranasal or buccal midazolam allows families to stop prolonged seizures at home with a rescue plan.

From a neurosurgical angle, refractory SE from a focal lesion, such as a cortical dysplasia or tumor, sometimes ends only with emergency resection.

keyPoints: SE: convulsive seizure ≥5 min (t1) or repeated seizures without recovery; injury likely after 30 min (t2).
GABA-A receptors internalize during prolonged seizures, so benzodiazepines lose potency over time.
First-line: benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam, IM/intranasal midazolam).
Second-line: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate (similar in ESETT).
Refractory: anesthetic infusions with continuous EEG in ICU.
Nonconvulsive SE needs EEG to diagnose; NORSE is often autoimmune.

examples.src: Generalized convulsion still going at 7 minutes in the field, no IV.
After convulsive SE, the patient stops shaking but stays unresponsive for 40 minutes.
Previously healthy young adult with fever days earlier, then refractory seizures.
examples.tr: NORSE/FIRES; consider autoimmune causes and immunotherapy.

lessons.title: Drug-Resistant Epilepsy

levels.kid:
Most people with epilepsy take medicine and their seizures stop. But for about one in three people, the medicines don't stop the seizures, even after trying a few different ones.

Then doctors become detectives. They watch seizures on video with brain-wave sensors and take special brain pictures to find the exact spot where seizures start.

If they find one small spot that the brain can live without, a surgeon can remove it, and many people become seizure-free. If not, doctors can use tiny brain pacemakers or a special diet to help.
levels.hs:
Drug-resistant epilepsy means seizures continue even after trying two appropriate seizure medicines, taken correctly at proper amounts. About a third of people with epilepsy fall into this group. After two drugs fail, the chance that a third drug will make someone seizure-free is small, only a few percent per new drug.

This matters because ongoing seizures carry real risks: injuries, memory and mood problems, being unable to drive, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP).

First, doctors check for 'pseudo-resistance': maybe the diagnosis is wrong (fainting or functional seizures), the wrong drug was chosen for the epilepsy type, or the medicine isn't being taken regularly.

Then comes a presurgical evaluation at an epilepsy center:
- Video-EEG monitoring to record seizures.
- High-resolution MRI to find a lesion.
- PET and other scans, and neuropsychological testing of memory and language.

Treatment options:
- Resective surgery: removing the area where seizures start. Temporal lobe surgery makes about 60 to 70 percent of well-selected patients seizure-free.
- Laser ablation: a thin laser probe heats and destroys the seizure focus through a tiny hole.
- Disconnection: cutting pathways, such as the corpus callosum for drop attacks.
- Neuromodulation: vagus nerve stimulation, responsive neurostimulation, and deep brain stimulation reduce seizures.
- The ketogenic diet, a very high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet, especially helpful in children.

Sadly, many people wait many years before being referred for surgery, even though it can work very well.
levels.college:
ILAE definition (2010): failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules (as monotherapy or in combination) to achieve sustained seizure freedom. Kwan and Brodie's classic cohort showed seizure freedom of about half with the first drug, a smaller fraction with the second, and only a few percent with each subsequent drug.

Presurgical evaluation aims to define the epileptogenic zone, the minimal area whose removal stops seizures, using converging data:
- Semiology on video-EEG.
- MRI (3 tesla, epilepsy protocol): hippocampal sclerosis, focal cortical dysplasia, low-grade tumors (ganglioglioma, DNET), cavernomas.
- FDG-PET: interictal hypometabolism, helpful in MRI-negative cases.
- Ictal SPECT: hyperperfusion during the seizure.
- MEG: localizes interictal spikes.
- Neuropsychology, functional MRI for language and memory lateralization, and sometimes the Wada test.
- Intracranial EEG (stereo-EEG or subdural grids) when noninvasive data are discordant.

Surgical options:
- Anterior temporal lobectomy or selective amygdalohippocampectomy: the Wiebe randomized trial (2001) showed 58 percent seizure-free with surgery versus 8 percent with continued medicines at one year. The ERSET trial showed benefit in early surgery.
- Lesionectomy for well-defined lesions.
- MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT): minimally invasive, less cognitive impact, somewhat lower seizure-freedom than open resection in mesial temporal epilepsy.
- Hemispherotomy for diffuse unilateral disease (Rasmussen encephalitis, hemimegalencephaly, perinatal stroke).
- Corpus callosotomy for drop attacks.
- Multiple subpial transections for eloquent cortex (rarely used now).

Neuromodulation (palliative, rarely seizure-free): vagus nerve stimulation; responsive neurostimulation (RNS), which detects seizure onset and delivers stimulation, allowing treatment of foci in eloquent cortex or bilateral mesial temporal onset; and deep brain stimulation of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (SANTE trial). Responses often improve over years.

Dietary therapy: ketogenic diet and modified Atkins diet; first-line for GLUT1 deficiency and pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency.
levels.phd:
Drug resistance has several competing explanations. The transporter hypothesis proposes overexpression of efflux pumps such as P-glycoprotein at the blood-brain barrier in epileptogenic tissue, lowering local drug concentrations. The target hypothesis proposes altered drug targets, for example reduced sensitivity of sodium channels to carbamazepine in hippocampal tissue from resistant patients. The intrinsic severity hypothesis argues that more severe epilepsy (high early seizure frequency) is inherently harder to treat. Network hypotheses suggest remodeled circuits, such as mossy fiber sprouting and interneuron loss in hippocampal sclerosis, generate seizures independent of the drug's target. These are not mutually exclusive, and drug resistance probably varies by etiology.

Focal cortical dysplasia, the most common lesion in pediatric epilepsy surgery, illustrates molecular causation: type II dysplasias with dysmorphic neurons and balloon cells result from somatic mutations in the mTOR pathway (MTOR, PIK3CA, DEPDC5, TSC1 and TSC2) in a subset of brain cells. A 'brain somatic mosaicism' framework explains why MRI-negative focal epilepsies can be genetically focal. Ultra-deep sequencing of resected tissue and even cell-free DNA from CSF or from electrodes after stereo-EEG are being explored to identify these mutations before surgery, which could guide targeted mTOR inhibition.

The epileptogenic zone is a theoretical construct: it cannot be measured directly, only inferred from the irritative zone (interictal spikes), seizure-onset zone, symptomatogenic zone, functional deficit zone and lesion. Postoperative seizure freedom is the only proof that it was removed. Network neuroscience reframes this: computational 'virtual brain' models built from a patient's connectivity and stereo-EEG predict which nodes to remove; a large trial in France tested this approach.

Closed-loop neuromodulation is reshaping theory as well. Long-term RNS recordings revealed multiday seizure cycles, often near weekly to monthly periodicity, and individualized seizure-risk forecasting based on these rhythms now appears feasible. This suggests treatment timed to risk could improve on continuous therapy.
levels.expert:
The most important fact about drug-resistant epilepsy is that it is undertreated surgically. The average delay from epilepsy onset to surgery has historically been around 20 years, while each year of uncontrolled seizures carries risks of injury, cognitive decline, social harm and SUDEP. The guideline-backed rule is simple: after two appropriate drugs fail, refer to a comprehensive epilepsy center.

In clinic:
- Confirm the diagnosis and the epilepsy type before calling it drug-resistant. Video-EEG often shows that some 'refractory' patients have functional seizures or syncope.
- Check adherence, interactions and the drug spectrum.
- Ask about SUDEP risk factors, especially frequent generalized tonic-clonic seizures and nocturnal seizures while alone, and discuss them honestly. Seizure detection devices and supervision at night may help.

The multidisciplinary surgical conference weighs:
- Concordance: do semiology, EEG, MRI, PET and neuropsychology point to the same place?
- Eloquence: will removal cost language, memory, motor or visual function? A dominant hemisphere patient with good verbal memory has more to lose from left temporal resection.
- Patient goals: seizure freedom, driving, work, cognitive priorities.

Technique choices: open resection gives the highest chance of seizure freedom for lesional temporal epilepsy; laser ablation offers quicker recovery and better naming preservation, at the price of somewhat lower seizure freedom; RNS fits bilateral or eloquent-cortex onsets. In children with catastrophic hemispheric epilepsy, an early hemispherotomy can preserve development, since the young brain reorganizes language and motor function well.

After surgery, seizure freedom is reassessed over years; many patients reduce medications, and some stop them under supervision.

keyPoints: Drug-resistant epilepsy: failure of two appropriate, tolerated medication trials.
About one-third of people with epilepsy are drug-resistant; additional drugs rarely achieve seizure freedom.
Rule out pseudo-resistance (wrong diagnosis, wrong drug, nonadherence).
Presurgical workup: video-EEG, MRI, PET, neuropsychology, sometimes intracranial EEG.
Temporal lobe surgery is far superior to continued medicines in selected patients.
Options also include LITT, hemispherotomy, callosotomy, VNS, RNS, DBS and ketogenic diet.
